title: A Gold Medal Forged by a Mother's Love
excerpt: Under the bright starry sky, Xiaopeng took out the gold medal and hung it around his mother's neck...

inline.s: Once you embrace hardship, hardship is no longer hard.
Under the bright starry sky, Xiaopeng took out the gold medal and hung it around his mother's neck

On July 28, 1997, An Jinpeng, a senior student at Tianjin No. 1 High School, won a gold medal at the 38th International Mathematical Olympiad held in Argentina, writing a new page in the history of Tianjin. Behind the success of this nineteen-year-old mathematical prodigy lies a story of a mother's love so great it brings tears to the eyes

September 5, 1997, was the day Xiaopeng left home to report to the Institute of Mathematics at Peking University. Early that morning, wisps of cooking smoke rose from the dilapidated farmhouse where Xiaopeng lived. His mother, limping, was boiling noodles — noodles she had obtained by trading five eggs with a neighbor. Her foot had been sprained two days earlier when she was pushing a cartload of vegetables toward town, trying to raise a little more money for Xiaopeng's tuition.

Holding the bowl, Xiaopeng wept. Setting down his chopsticks, he knelt on the ground and for a long while stroked his mother's foot, which was swollen higher than a steamed bun, his tears falling drop by drop onto the floor
Xiaopeng's home was in Dayoudai Village, Wuqing County, Tianjin, and he had a mother who was the greatest in the world — her name was Li Yanxia.

Xiaopeng's family was very poor. When he was born, his grandmother fell ill and was bedridden on the kang. When he was four, his grandfather contracted bronchial asthma and suffered a stroke that left him half-paralyzed. Expenses within and without caused the family's debts to grow year after year.

At seven, Xiaopeng started school. His tuition was borrowed by his mother. Xiaopeng would always pick up the pencil stubs his classmates threw away, tie them to a small stick with string, and keep using them, or rub his used exercise books clean with an eraser and use them again. His mother, who cherished him deeply, sometimes even had to borrow a few cents to buy pencils and notebooks.

But his mother also had moments of joy: in every exam, large or small, Xiaopeng always ranked first, and in mathematics he always scored full marks. Encouraged by his mother, Xiaopeng found more and more joy in study, and truly knew of nothing in the world more delightful than reading.

Before even entering primary school, Xiaopeng had mastered the four arithmetic operations, fractions, and decimals. In primary school, he taught himself the mathematics, physics, and chemistry of the junior-high level. In junior high, he finished the senior-high science curriculum on his own. In May 1994, when Tianjin held a junior-high physics competition, Xiaopeng was the only child from the countryside, among the students of the five suburban counties, to place in the top three.

That June, Xiaopeng was admitted to the renowned Tianjin No. 1 High School as an exceptional case. Overjoyed, he rushed straight home — only to find that when he told his family the good news, their faces were clouded with worry. His grandmother had passed away less than half a year earlier, his grandfather was critically ill, and the family now owed more than ten thousand yuan. Silently, Xiaopeng returned to his room and wept all day.

That evening, he heard quarreling outside the room. His mother wanted to sell the family donkey so that Xiaopeng could go to school, but his father was firmly opposed. Their words reached the ears of his gravely ill grandfather, who, in his distress, suddenly passed away forever.

After the grandfather was laid to rest, the family owed several thousand yuan more. Xiaopeng never mentioned schooling again; he folded up the admission letter, tucked it into his pillowcase, and went to the fields every day to help his mother farm. Two days later, Xiaopeng and his father discovered at the same time that the little donkey was gone. His father, face livid, demanded of his mother: “Did you sell the little donkey? Have you lost your mind? From now on, when we tend the crops and sell the grain, will you push the cart by hand and carry the loads on your shoulders? That few hundred yuan from the donkey — can it keep Jinpeng in school for one term or two

That day, his mother wept, and in a fierce, fierce voice she shouted at his father: “What is wrong with Peng'er wanting to study? His getting into the city's No. 1 High School is the only one in all of Wuqing County. We must not let the word ‘poor’ ruin our son's future. Even if I have to push by hand and carry on my shoulders, I will keep him in school

Holding the six hundred yuan his mother had gotten from selling the donkey, Xiaopeng longed to kneel down and kowtow to her. He loved studying so much — yet once he continued, how many more hardships would his mother have to endure, how much more suffering to bear?

That autumn, when Xiaopeng went home for his winter clothes, he found his father lying on the kang, his face sallow, thin as skin and bones. His mother told him as if nothing were wrong: “It's nothing — a bad cold, almost better now.” But the next day, when Xiaopeng picked up the medicine bottle and read the English on it, he discovered the pills were for suppressing cancer cells. He drew his mother outside and tearfully asked what was happening. His mother said that ever since he had entered the No. 1 High School, his father had begun passing blood, worse by the day. She had borrowed six thousand yuan and taken him to Tianjin and Beijing again and again for checkups; at last he was diagnosed with intestinal polyps, and the doctor urged him to have surgery soon. She was about to borrow more money, but his father absolutely refused, saying that they had already borrowed from every relative and friend — who would be willing to lend to them again when they only borrowed and never repaid?

That day, a neighbor also told Xiaopeng that his mother had completed the harvest in a primitive and tragic way. Not strong enough to carry the wheat to the threshing ground, and with no money to hire help, she cut it patch by patch, then hauled it home on a handcart. At night she spread a plastic sheet in the yard and, with both hands, grabbed great handfuls of wheat stalks and beat them against a big stone
The three mu of wheat depended entirely on her alone. When she was too exhausted to stand, she cut on her knees; her knees were worn raw and bleeding, and she walked with an unsteady sway
, and before the neighbor had even finished, Xiaopeng ran flying home and cried out loud: “Mother, Mother, I can't go on studying anymore!”

In the end, his mother still drove Xiaopeng back to school. His living allowance was sixty to eighty yuan a month — pitifully little compared with his classmates' two hundred to two hundred forty. But only Xiaopeng knew that at the start of every month his mother had to save penny by penny and sell eggs and vegetables yuan by yuan; and when she truly could not scrape enough together, she had to borrow twenty or thirty more. His mother, father, and younger brother almost never ate vegetables; even the little they had was not dressed with oil, only stirred with a bit of brine from pickled vegetables.

So that Xiaopeng would not go hungry, his mother walked more than ten li every month to buy instant noodles for him at wholesale. At the end of every month, she would come to Tianjin bearing a bulging bag, having endured endless hardships on the journey. Besides the instant noodles, the bag held waste paper she had gotten from a printing plant six li away (to serve as Xiaopeng's scratch paper), a big jar of soybean chili paste, salted mustard strips, and a pair of hair clippers. (The cheapest haircut in Tianjin cost five yuan, and his mother wanted Xiaopeng to save that money for a few extra steamed buns.)

Xiaopeng was the only student at Tianjin No. 1 High School who could not afford even vegetables in the cafeteria; he could only buy two steamed buns and, back in his dorm, soak some instant noodles with chili paste and pickles. He was also the only student who could not afford draft paper, doing his calculations on waste paper printed on one side, and the only one who had never used soap, washing his clothes with a bit of soda ash begged from the cafeteria. Yet Xiaopeng was never ashamed. He felt that his mother was a hero who battled hardship and misfortune, and that to be her son was his supreme honor.

When he first entered Tianjin No. 1 High School, the very first English class left Xiaopeng completely bewildered. When his mother came, he told her of his worry that he could not keep up in English, and to his surprise she answered with a beaming smile: “Mother only knows that you are a child who endures hardship best, and Mother does not like to hear you say it is hard.
Because once you embrace hardship, it is no longer hard
.” Xiaopeng remembered his mother's words.

Xiaopeng stammered a little, and someone told him that to learn English well, one must first make one's tongue obey one's will. So he would often put a pebble in his mouth and then recite English with all his might. His tongue and the pebble rubbed and rubbed; sometimes bloodied water trickled from the corner of his mouth, but Xiaopeng always gritted his teeth and held on.

Half a year passed; the little pebble was worn smooth, and Xiaopeng's tongue was worn flat, while his English rose into the top three of his class. Xiaopeng was truly grateful to his mother; her words had spurred him to surmount, miraculously, so great an obstacle to his learning.

In 1996, Xiaopeng competed for the first time in the Tianjin division of the National Olympiad of Knowledge, winning first prize in physics and second prize in mathematics, and was chosen to represent Tianjin at the national physics Olympiad in Hangzhou.

To win a national first prize for Mother, and then go on to compete in the world mathematics and science competition.” Unable to contain his excitement, Xiaopeng wrote to his mother with the good news and his wish.

In the end, Xiaopeng won only a second prize. He threw himself onto his bed and would neither eat nor drink, even though it was already the best result among the contestants from Tianjin. To repay a mother who had endured such hardship, it truly was not enough!

Back at school, his teachers helped Xiaopeng analyze the reasons for his failure. He had always wanted to develop himself across mathematics, physics, and chemistry, and had taken on too many main subjects, scattering his energy. If he now focused on mathematics alone, he would surely make it.
In January 1997, Xiaopeng at last won first place with a perfect score in the national mathematics Olympiad, entered the national training team smoothly, and came out on top in ten successive tests.

According to the rules, Xiaopeng had to bear his own expenses for the trip to Argentina. After paying the registration fee, he wrapped up his essential books and the soybean chili paste his mother had made, and his preparations were done. His homeroom teacher and math teacher saw that Xiaopeng still wore clothes handed to him by others — mismatched in color and size — and opened the storage cabinet, pointing at the padded jacket whose sleeves had been lengthened twice and whose hem had been let down three inches, and at the patched and repatched undershirts and vests: “Jinpeng, are these all the clothes you have?” Not knowing what to do, Xiaopeng quickly said: “Teacher, I am not afraid of losing face. My mother always told me, ‘when the belly is full of poetry and books, one's bearing shines of itself.' Wearing these, I would not be afraid even to meet Clinton in America.”

On July 27, the Olympiad officially began. From eight thirty in the morning until two in the afternoon, Xiaopeng worked on the problems for a full five and a half hours. The results were announced the next day. First came the bronze medals; Xiaopeng did not wish to hear his name. Next the silver medals were announced; and finally, the gold medals — one, two, and the third was Xiaopeng. He wept for joy, and cried out silently in his heart: “Mother, your son has succeeded.”

That very night, the news that Xiaopeng and another classmate had won the gold and silver medals at the 38th International Mathematical Olympiad was broadcast by China National Radio and China Central Television. On August 1, when Xiaopeng returned bearing honors, the China Association for Science and Technology and the Chinese Mathematical Society held a grand welcoming ceremony for him. At that moment Xiaopeng wanted to go home, to see his mother as soon as possible, and with his own hands to hang the gleaming gold medal around her neck.

That night, after ten o'clock, Xiaopeng at last groped his way home through the dark — the home he had yearned for day and night. It was his father who opened the door, but it was still his kind mother who swept him into her arms and held him tight. Under the bright, star-filled sky, his mother held Xiaopeng so close
, and Xiaopeng took out the gold medal, hung it around her neck, and wept freely.

On August 12, the auditorium of Tianjin No. 1 High School was filled to the last seat. His mother sat on the rostrum together with officials of the city education bureau and renowned professors of mathematics. That day, Xiaopeng spoke these words:

“I want to thank one person with my whole life, and that is the mother who raised me to adulthood. She is an ordinary peasant woman, yet the principles of life she taught me can inspire me for a lifetime. In my first year of senior high, I wanted to buy a Chinese-English Dictionary to study English. Mother had no money in her pocket, yet she still promised to find a way. After breakfast, Mother borrowed a cart, loaded it with cabbages, and together with me dragged it to the county seat forty li away to sell them. By the time we reached the county seat, it was nearly noon. Mother and I had drunk only two bowls of sweet-potato and corn gruel in the morning, and my stomach was growling with hunger; I wished desperately that a buyer would come at once and take the vegetables away. But Mother still bargained patiently, and at last sold them at ten fen per jin. Two hundred ten jin of cabbage should have brought twenty-one yuan, but the buyer gave only twenty. With money in hand I wanted to eat first, but Mother said, let's buy the book first — that is today's proper business. We went to the bookstore and asked the price: eighteen yuan and twenty-five fen. After buying the book, only one yuan and seventy-five fen remained. Mother gave me only seventy-five fen in small change to buy two baked buns, saying the remaining one yuan had to be saved for my schooling. Although I ate two buns, by the time the two of us had nearly walked the forty-odd li home, I was already faint and dizzy with hunger. Only then did I remember that I had actually forgotten to share a bun with Mother, who had gone hungry all day and pulled the cart eighty li for me. I was filled with regret, but Mother said: ‘Mother doesn't have much education, but Mother remembers a line of Gorky's that the teacher read aloud when I was little — “poverty is the best university.” If you can pass the test in this school, then the universities of Tianjin and Beijing are yours to enter.' As Mother spoke, she did not look at me; she gazed far down that dirt road, as if it truly could lead to Tianjin, lead to Beijing. As I listened, I felt my stomach no longer hungry and my legs no longer sore
. If poverty is the best university, then I must say that my mother, a peasant woman, is the best teacher of my life.”
Below the stage, countless pairs of eyes grew moist. Xiaopeng turned around and bowed deeply to his mother, whose temples had already turned gray
